title: De praedestinatione: title — Rom 9:18 and Calvin
latin: DISSERTATIO DE PRAEDESTINATIONE ET REPROBATIONE. Per Reverendissimum virum JOANNEM DAVENANTIUM, Nuper Episcopum SARISBURIENSEM, Ante aliquot annos in celeberrima Academia Cantabrigiensi Theologiae Professorem in Scholis Theologicis auditoribus suis dictata. Rom. IX. 18. Cujus vult, miseretur: & quem vult, indurat. Calvin. in Rom. IX. 18. Minime dubium est, Paulum e suo ipsius sensu haec loqui, Deum scilicet PRO ARBITRIO SUO, quem visum illi fuerit, misericordia dignari: in quemcunque libuerit judicii severitatem stringere. Ex Officina Rogeri Danielis, Alma Academiae Cantabrigiensis Typographi, 1650.
pass_a: DISSERTATION ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. By the Most Reverend man John Davenant, lately Bishop of Salisbury, some years earlier Professor of Theology in the most celebrated University of Cambridge, dictated in the Theological Schools to his hearers. Romans 9:18. Of whom he wills, he has mercy: and whom he wills, he hardens. Calvin on Romans 9:18. There is least doubt that Paul speaks these things from his own sense, namely that God BY HIS OWN ARBITRARY WILL deigns with mercy whom it has seemed good to him; against whomever it has pleased he draws tight the severity of judgment. From the workshop of Roger Daniel, Printer of the nurturing University of Cambridge, 1650.
pass_b: A DISSERTATION ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. By the Most Reverend John Davenant, lately Bishop of Salisbury, formerly Professor of Theology in the University of Cambridge, delivered in the Theological Schools to his hearers. [[Romans 9:18 >> Bible:Romans 9:18]]. Of whom he wills, he has mercy; and whom he wills, he hardens. Calvin on Romans 9:18: There is scarcely any doubt that Paul speaks here in his own sense — that God, by his own free decision, shows mercy to whom he chooses, and draws the severity of judgment against whomever he pleases. Printed at Cambridge by Roger Daniel, University Printer, 1650.

title: Prefatio: return to theological labor; scope of the inquiry
latin: Prefatio habita ad Academicos. Quod de agricolis dixit Poeta, Redit agricolis labor actus in orbem, Georg. 2, id Theologis verius convenit; ac praesertim illis quibus ipsa Cathedra laboris & sudoris necessitatem, non otii aut quietis opportunitatem subministrat. Hos igitur circulos orbesque laboris Theologici, quos mihi pro officii mei ratione conficiendos video, alacri & lubenti animo ingrediar: Deumque inprimis precabor, ut me sic dirigat in toto hoc operis suscipiendi curriculo, ne vel tantillum deflectam ab immobili illo centro sacrae veritatis. Est autem opus quod aggredior in se arduum, multisque difficultatibus obstructum. Quid enim altius, aut ab humanis sensibus remotius, quam illud aeternum decretum praedestinationis Divinae, quo ante jacta mundi fundamenta quosdam prae aliis, imo aliis plane praeteritis, ad vitam aeternam in Christo participandam electos confitemur? Huic negotio explicando operam nostram addiximus; ea tamen lege, ne quis vestrum exspectet ut vel omnes quaestiones, quae in hac materia tractantur a Theologis, attingam (immensi hoc, addo etiam, & supervacui laboris esset), vel ullas omnino ex illis curiosis quaestiunculis, quibus malesani homunciones seipsos torquere, alios vexare, fidem denique Christianam obscurare solent & pervertere. Respuit enim captiosas & inutiles quaestiones fides constans; &, quisquis fidelis vere audit, Divinae sapientiae se religiosum ostendit, non libidinosum suae, Hilar. 1. De Trinit. ut graviter Tertullianus, De Resurr. Proponemus ergo nobis in hac disquisitione nostra paucula quaedam ex maxime necessariis tractanda; eaque non rimabimur altius quam quo Scriptura praelucente penetremus. Huic regulae si adhaerescamus, doctrinam hanc praedestinationis non modo inter eruditos proponendam, sed ipsi populo divulgandam, recte & sapienter judicavit Augustinus, De persev. sanctor. lib. 2. cap. 16. idque ita fieri posse docuit, ut id quod dicitur, & parvulis lac, & grandibus esca sit.
pass_a: Preface held before the Academics. What the Poet said of farmers, The labor done returns for farmers in a circle, Georgics 2, that agrees more truly with theologians; and especially with those to whom the Chair itself supplies the necessity of labor and sweat, not an opportunity of leisure or quiet. These circles and orbs of Theological labor, therefore, which I see must be completed by me according to the account of my office, I will enter with eager and willing mind: and first I will pray God that he so direct me in this whole course of the work to be undertaken, that I may not deflect even a little from that immovable center of sacred truth. But the work which I approach is in itself steep, and blocked with many difficulties. For what is higher, or more remote from human senses, than that eternal decree of Divine predestination, by which before the foundations of the world were laid we confess certain ones elected before others, indeed with others plainly passed by, to share eternal life in Christ? To explaining this business we have devoted our labor; yet under this law, lest any of you expect that I either touch all the questions which are treated by theologians in this matter (that would be of immense, I add also of superfluous, labor), or any at all of those curious little questions by which unhealthy little men are wont to torture themselves, vex others, and finally obscure and pervert the Christian faith. For constant faith rejects captious and useless questions; and whoever truly hears as a believer shows himself religious toward Divine wisdom, not lustful toward his own, Hilary 1 On the Trinity, as Tertullian gravely, On the Resurrection. We will therefore set before ourselves in this our inquiry a few things from the most necessary to be treated; and those we will not probe deeper than where Scripture giving light we may penetrate. If we cling to this rule, Augustine rightly and wisely judged this doctrine of predestination ought to be proposed not only among the learned, but published to the people itself, On the Perseverance of the Saints book 2 chapter 16; and he taught it can be done so that what is said is both milk for little ones and food for the grown.
pass_b: Preface delivered to the University. What the poet said of farmers — "The finished labor returns for farmers in a circle" (Georgics 2) — fits theologians still more truly, especially those whose chair itself demands labor and sweat, not leisure or quiet. So I will enter these rounds of theological work that my office requires, eager and willing; and I will ask God first to steer me through the whole course of this undertaking so that I do not swerve even a little from the fixed center of sacred truth. The work I take up is steep in itself and blocked with many difficulties. For what is higher, or farther from human sense, than that eternal decree of Divine predestination by which, before the world's foundations were laid, we confess that certain ones were chosen before others — indeed with others plainly passed by — to share eternal life in Christ? We have given our labor to explaining that business, yet under this rule: let no one of you expect that I will touch every question theologians treat in this matter (that would be immense labor, and superfluous too), or any of those curious little puzzles by which unhealthy little men torture themselves, vex others, and finally obscure and twist the Christian faith. Steady faith rejects captious and useless questions; and whoever truly hears as a believer shows himself devout toward Divine wisdom, not craving his own (Hilary, On the Trinity 1; so also Tertullian, On the Resurrection). In this inquiry, then, we will set ourselves only a few of the most necessary points, and we will not dig deeper than Scripture's light lets us go. If we keep to that rule, Augustine rightly judged that this doctrine of predestination should be taught not only among the learned but also to the people (On the Perseverance of the Saints 2.16), and that it can be said so as to be milk for little ones and solid food for the grown.

title: Prefatio: preach free election; Pontifical reduction of the mystery
latin: Si Pauli vestigia premamus, si sancti Augustini exemplum imitemur, si doctrinae in hac Ecclesia nostra receptae adhaerescamus, nullum scandali periculum est. E contra, si obrui & sepeliri patiamur doctrinam gratuita electionis, aut (quod turpius est) si illam a quibusdam Pontificiis aliisque pessime corruptam & in contrarium detortam aequo animo feramus, non carebit utique suspicione haec iners taciturnitas: occurreret enim nobis expedita defensio veritatis, si falsitas promulgata displiceret. Neminem vestrum latere arbitror, ex Pontificiis scriptoribus multos, totum hoc mysterium electionis & reprobationis, in quo Paulus obstupuit, ad nimis claram facilemque discriminis rationem revocasse, dum alios ex praescientia meritorum electos, alios autem ex praescientia demeritorum rejectos philosophorum.
pass_a: If we press Paul's footsteps, if we imitate the example of holy Augustine, if we cling to the doctrine received in this our Church, there is no danger of scandal. On the contrary, if we suffer the doctrine of free election to be overwhelmed and buried, or (what is baser) if we bear with equal mind that doctrine corrupted worst by certain Pontificals and others and twisted into the contrary, this inert silence will certainly not lack suspicion: for a ready defense of truth would meet us, if promulgated falsehood were displeasing. I think it is hidden from none of you that many from the Pontifical writers have recalled this whole mystery of election and reprobation, at which Paul stood astonished, to an all-too-clear and easy account of the difference, while they philosophize that some are elected from foreknowledge of merits, but others rejected from foreknowledge of demerits.
pass_b: If we follow Paul's steps, imitate holy Augustine, and hold the doctrine received in this our Church, there is no danger of scandal. But if we let the doctrine of free election be overwhelmed and buried — or, worse, if we calmly endure it when certain Papal writers and others have badly corrupted it and twisted it the other way — that lazy silence will not escape suspicion. A ready defense of the truth would meet us if published falsehood displeased us. None of you, I think, fails to see that many Papal writers have reduced this whole mystery of election and reprobation — at which Paul stood astonished — to an all-too-clear and easy account of the difference, teaching that some are chosen from foreknowledge of merits, others rejected from foreknowledge of demerits.

title: Prefatio close: Arminian fabric; elect unto faith; Anglican defense
latin: Et quod magis dolendum est, e schola Arminiana prodierunt novelli doctores, qui fundatissimam Ecclesiae catholicae doctrinam labefactare conantur, & novam nescio quam atque orthodoxis Ecclesiis plane incognitam electionis & reprobationis fabricam exstruere. Quod Papistae praevisis operibus, id isti fidei & infidelitati praevisae assignandum putant: Et sic demum Divinae justitiae prospectum opinantur, si ante jacta mundi fundamenta eos tantum elegisse dicatur, quos ad oblatam vocationis gratiam credituros, & in fide ad extremum usque perseveraturos praeviderit; Ex adverso eos solos statuatur reprobasse, quos gratiam repulsuros, incredulos, & in incredulitate morituros praesciverit. Bellos scilicet Theologos, qui hominem fide prius justificatum, & in adoptionis & salutis statu positum, quam a Deo praedestinatum, aut ad salutem in Christo electum introducunt! Praeclaros gratiae Divinae praecones, qui discrimen bonarum & malarum voluntatum in credendo aut non credendo nolunt ad Dei eligentis specialem erga credentes misericordiam reducere: Sed quicquid hoc discriminis est, satagunt ad contingentem liberi arbitrii actum in admittenda, retinenda & exercenda gratia revocare. Quanto melius, & ad mentem Apostoli accommodatius Pelagianorum flagellum Augustinus de praedest. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17. Elegit Deus fideles, sed ut fiant, non quia jam erant. Eligendo facit divites in fide, sicut heredes regni. Fuit igitur post Pelagium exortum Augustini atque omnium adeo Catholicorum explicata ac rata sententia, homines fuisse electos non ex operibus, sed ad opera bona, non ex fide, sed ad fidem. Hoc est, qui electi sunt fideles & bonorum operum studiosi evaserunt; non quia tales futuri praevidebantur a Deo, electi fuerunt. Hanc doctrinam in Scholis propugnare, hanc in Ecclesiis praedicare oportet. Nam cum Pontificii alii errorum suorum venena passim diffundunt, nos etiam haud minore industria paremus nostris salutaria antidota. Notum est illud Aristotelis, &c. Nos etiam turpe ducamus in causa Dei obmutescere, cum hostes veritatis scriptis & clamoribus suis undique nobis obstrepant. Ne igitur vicini erroris contagio & nostros tandem corripiat, pro meae tenuitatis modulo suscipiam explicationem verissimae ejus doctrinae, quam Ecclesia haec Anglicana in praedestinationis negotio suis omnibus amplectandam commendavit. Refellam etiam pro virili illa sophismata, quibus adversarii sanam Ecclesiae doctrinam subvertere, atque nova sua commenta stabilire moliuntur.
pass_a: And what is more to be lamented, from the Arminian school there have come forth new doctors, who try to shake the most well-founded doctrine of the catholic Church, and to build I-know-not-what new fabric of election and reprobation, plainly unknown to orthodox Churches. What the Papists assign to foreseen works, these think must be assigned to foreseen faith and unbelief: And so at last they think they have looked out for Divine justice, if before the foundations of the world were laid he is said to have elected only those whom he foresaw would believe toward the offered grace of calling, and would persevere in faith clear to the end; On the contrary, let it be stated that he reprobated only those whom he foreknew would repulse grace, unbelieving, and would die in unbelief. Fine theologians indeed, who introduce a man first justified by faith, and placed in the state of adoption and salvation, before he is predestined by God, or elected to salvation in Christ! Splendid heralds of Divine grace, who refuse to reduce the difference of good and bad wills in believing or not believing to the special mercy of God electing toward believers: But whatever this difference is, they strive to recall it to the contingent act of free choice in admitting, retaining, and exercising grace. How much better, and more fitted to the Apostle's mind, is Augustine the scourge of the Pelagians On the Predestination of the Saints book 1 chapter 17: God elected the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By electing he makes them rich in faith, as heirs of the kingdom. There was therefore after Pelagius arose the explained and ratified opinion of Augustine and of all Catholics accordingly, that human beings were elected not from works but unto good works, not from faith but unto faith. That is, those who are elect came out faithful and devoted to good works; they were not elected because such ones were foreseen by God as about to be. This doctrine must be defended in the Schools, this preached in the Churches. For when other Pontificals pour out the poisons of their errors everywhere, let us also with no less industry prepare salutary antidotes for our people. That saying of Aristotle is known, etc. Let us also count it shameful to grow mute in God's cause, when enemies of the truth with writings and clamors shout against us on every side. Lest therefore the contagion of neighboring error seize ours too at last, according to the measure of my thinness I will undertake the explanation of that most true doctrine which this Anglican Church has recommended to all her own to be embraced in the business of predestination. I will also refute as far as I can those sophisms by which adversaries strive to overthrow the sound doctrine of the Church, and to establish their new fictions.
pass_b: And what hurts more: from the Arminian school new teachers have come out who try to shake the catholic Church's most settled doctrine, and to raise I know not what new fabric of election and reprobation, wholly unknown to orthodox churches. What Papists assign to foreseen works, these assign to foreseen faith and unbelief. So they think they have secured Divine justice if, before the world's foundations were laid, God is said to have chosen only those he foresaw would believe the offered call and persevere in faith to the end; and, on the other side, to have reprobated only those he foreknew would refuse grace, remain unbelieving, and die in unbelief. Fine theologians indeed — who bring in a man already justified by faith, already set in adoption and salvation, before God has predestined him or chosen him to salvation in Christ! Splendid heralds of Divine grace — who will not trace the difference of good and bad wills in believing or not believing to the electing God's special mercy toward believers, but strain to refer whatever difference there is to a contingent act of free choice in admitting, keeping, and exercising grace. How much better — and closer to the Apostle's mind — is Augustine, scourge of the Pelagians (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By choosing he makes them rich in faith, as heirs of the kingdom." So after Pelagius arose, Augustine and Catholics generally held and ratified this: people were chosen not from works but unto good works, not from faith but unto faith. That is: the elect became faithful and eager for good works; they were not chosen because God foresaw they would be such. This doctrine must be defended in the schools and preached in the churches. When Papal writers pour out their error's poisons everywhere, let us with no less care prepare antidotes for our own. Aristotle's saying is known. Let us also count it shameful to fall silent in God's cause while enemies of the truth shout against us on every side with writings and noise. Lest neighboring error's contagion seize ours too, I will, according to my slender measure, undertake to explain that most true doctrine which this Church of England has commended to all her people to embrace in the matter of predestination. And as far as I can I will refute those sophisms by which adversaries try to overturn the Church's sound teaching and to settle their new inventions.

title: Cap. 1 Prolegomena: four points before the controversy
latin: Cap. I. Prolegomena. Sed quo tota haec res in lucem proferatur facilius, non abs re erit ipsi disputationi praemittere nonnulla, quorum explicatio viam sternet huic controversiae intelligendae. Primo igitur, quia in illis quaestionibus quae de praedestinatione aguntur, aut reprobatione, maximas lites parit ipse ordo considerationis nostrae, dum alius contendit in intellectu & decretis Divinis illud esse prius, quod alius opinatur esse posterius, de tota hac ratione prioritatis & posterioritatis quoad diversa signa rationis, paucis differendum est. Secundo, quia ipsa vocabula Electionis, Praedestinationis, Reprobationis, diversimode a diversis usurpantur, necesse erit ipsam vocabulorum vim explanare, & quo sensu ab aliis, quo a nobis accipiantur, ostendere. Tertio, quia de qualitatibus sive conditionibus subjecti, diversi diverso modo philosophantur, operae pretium erit exponere, quid absolute requiratur & praesupponitur in ipso subjecto praedestinationis aut reprobationis promiscue considerato. Ultimo, quia praeter conditiones communes, quae ex aequo & indiscriminatim requiruntur, sive quis praedestinationis sive reprobationis subjectum statuatur, nonnulli insuper qualitates sive conditiones distinguentes ponunt, pro quarum discrimine actus praedestinationis Divinae in unum cadat, actus reprobationis in alterum, de hisce etiam, quam vim habeant, dispiciendum erit. Nam aliqui qui discrimen electionis & reprobationis ad hujusmodi, sive qualitates sive actus nostros, referunt, non patiuntur tamen ut causae appellentur, multo minus ut merita, imo non nisi gravate concedunt, ut vel conditiones praedestinationis nostrae nuncupentur. Sed ad rem accingamur: & ordiamur ab illis signis sive diversis instantibus, quae a Theologis assignari & distingui solent secundum ordinem prioris & posterioris, in actibus tum intellectus tum voluntatis Divinae.
pass_a: Chapter I. Prolegomena. But that this whole matter may be brought into the light more easily, it will not be beside the point to send ahead of the dispute itself some things, whose explanation will lay a road for understanding this controversy. First therefore, because in those questions which are driven about predestination, or reprobation, the very order of our consideration begets the greatest quarrels, while one contends that in the Divine intellect and decrees that is prior which another thinks is posterior, about this whole account of priority and posteriority as to diverse signs of reason, it must be discussed in a few words. Second, because the very words Election, Predestination, Reprobation are used diversely by diverse people, it will be necessary to explain the force of the words themselves, and to show in what sense they are taken by others, in what by us. Third, because about the qualities or conditions of the subject diverse people philosophize in diverse ways, it will be worth the labor to set out what is absolutely required and presupposed in the subject itself of predestination or reprobation considered promiscuously. Last, because besides the common conditions which are required equally and without discrimination, whether someone is set as subject of predestination or of reprobation, some further place distinguishing qualities or conditions, according to whose difference the act of Divine predestination falls on one, the act of reprobation on another, about these also, what force they have, it will have to be examined. For some who refer the difference of election and reprobation to things of this kind, whether our qualities or acts, yet do not suffer them to be called causes, much less merits, indeed only grudgingly concede that they even be named conditions of our predestination. But let us gird ourselves to the matter: and let us begin from those signs or diverse instants which theologians are wont to assign and distinguish according to the order of prior and posterior in the acts both of the Divine intellect and of the Divine will.
pass_b: Chapter I. Prolegomena. But so that this whole matter may come into the light more easily, it will not be out of place to set a few things before the dispute itself — things whose explanation will open the way into this controversy. First: in questions of predestination or reprobation the very order of our thought breeds the sharpest fights, while one claims that in God's intellect and decrees this is prior which another holds is posterior. So we must speak briefly of this whole account of priority and posteriority under the diverse signs of reason. Second: because the words Election, Predestination, and Reprobation are used differently by different writers, we must explain the force of the words themselves, and show in what sense others take them, and in what sense we do. Third: because writers argue differently about the qualities or conditions of the subject, it will be worth setting out what is absolutely required and presupposed in the subject of predestination or reprobation when that subject is considered in common. Last: besides the common conditions required equally and without distinction whether someone is made the subject of predestination or of reprobation, some place further distinguishing qualities or conditions, by whose difference the act of Divine predestination falls on one and the act of reprobation on another. Those too must be weighed for what force they have. For some who refer the difference of election and reprobation to such things — whether our qualities or our acts — still will not let them be called causes, much less merits, and only grudgingly allow them even to be named conditions of our predestination. But let us gird for the work, and begin from those signs or distinct instants that theologians usually assign and separate according to prior and posterior order in the acts of both the Divine intellect and the Divine will.

title: Prolegomena I: one eternal act in God; James 1:17; Ambrose and Hilary
latin: Primo igitur sciendum & tenendum est, si Dei naturam & perfectionem in se consideremus, illum non prius unum videre, dein aliud; neque prius hoc decernere aut velle, deinde illud; sed unico & simplicissimo actu ab aeterno omnia simul vidisse, omnia simul in se decrevisse. Ratio firmissima petitur ab immutabilitate Divina, Jacob. 1. 17. Apud Deum non est transmutatio, aut vicissitudinis obumbratio. Quae verba omnem mutationem sive in essendo, sive in operando a Divina natura excludunt. Nam si fingamus Deum quasi per vices agere in illis operationibus quae in Deo immanentes intelliguntur, ita ut prius hoc intelligat, deinde illud, prius hoc velit, deinde aliud; ponimus in Deo mutationem a potentia in actum: quae ejus absolutissimae simplicitati adversatur. Recte igitur Ambrosius, sed quicunque alius Autor fuerit, lib. 2. De vocat. Gent. cap. 10. Non est in Deo accidens, motus, aut nova voluntas, aut temporale consilium, nec cogitatio ejus cum rerum mutabilium inaequalitate variatur, sed cuncta pariter tempora & temporalia sempiterno ac stabili comprehendit intuitu. Adstipulatur etiam Hilarius, qui negat in Deo particulatas rerum cogitationes, atque asserit omnia penes Deum aequabili aeternitatis infinitate consistere, de Trin. 12. pag. 193. Assentiuntur Scholastici & Theologi omnes quos ego viderim, extra unum Vorstium, cujus deliria indigna sunt quae vel refutentur in Schola Theologica.
pass_a: First therefore it must be known and held, if we consider God's nature and perfection in itself, that he does not first see one thing, then another; nor first decree or will this, then that; but by one most simple act from eternity has seen all things at once, has decreed all things at once in himself. The firmest reason is sought from Divine immutability, James 1:17. With God there is not change, or shadow of turning. Which words exclude every change either in being or in working from the Divine nature. For if we feign that God acts as if by turns in those operations which are understood as immanent in God, so that he first understands this, then that, first wills this, then another; we place in God a change from potency into act: which stands against his most absolute simplicity. Rightly therefore Ambrose — or whoever else the author was — book 2 On the Calling of the Gentiles chapter 10: There is not in God accident, motion, or new will, or temporal counsel, nor is his thought varied with the inequality of changeable things, but he comprehends all times and temporal things alike with everlasting and stable intuition. Hilary also agrees, who denies particularized thoughts of things in God, and asserts that all things stand with God in the equal infinity of eternity, On the Trinity 12, page 193. All the Scholastics and theologians I have seen assent, except one Vorstius, whose ravings are unworthy even to be refuted in the Theological School.
pass_b: First, then, this must be known and held: if we consider God's nature and perfection in itself, he does not first see one thing and then another, nor first decree or will this and then that. By one most simple act from eternity he has seen all things at once and decreed all things at once in himself. The firmest ground is Divine immutability — [[James 1:17 >> Bible:James 1:17]]: with God there is no change, or shadow of turning. Those words shut every change — in being or in working — out of the Divine nature. If we imagine God acting by turns in those operations understood as immanent in him, so that he first understands this then that, first wills this then another, we place in God a move from potency into act — which contradicts his most absolute simplicity. So Ambrose is right (or whoever wrote book 2 of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 10): In God there is no accident, motion, new will, or temporal counsel; his thought is not varied by the inequality of changeable things; he comprehends all times and temporal things together with an everlasting, steady gaze. Hilary agrees: he denies piecemeal thoughts of things in God, and holds that all things stand with God in the even infinity of eternity (On the Trinity 12, p. 193). Every Scholastic and theologian I have seen assents — except one Vorstius, whose ravings are not even worth refuting in a theological school.

title: Prolegomena II: signs of priority among decrees; Scotus, Occam, Biel, Bannes
latin: Secundo, utcunque omnes actus in mente & voluntate Divina sint aeterni, & proinde ne levissimo quidem prioritatis & posterioritatis momento separemur; tamen, ex parte ipsarum rerum quas Deus intelligit & decrevit, signa quaedam prioritatis & posterioritatis distingui possunt, secundum nostrum modum intelligendi. Et hoc sensu quaeritur inter Theologos, utrum Deus prius decreverit dare electis vitam aeternam, an fidem & obedientiam, quae ducant ad vitam aeternam; & utrum prius aliquos reprobaverit & rejecerit a vita aeterna, quam lapsos & peccato contaminatos praeviderit. Atque hinc est quod fere omnes qui de praedestinatione & reprobatione scripserunt, seriem quandam, & quasi tabellam describunt, in qua ordinem decretorum Divinorum conantur delineare: non quod secundum rem in ipso Deo unum altero prius aut posterius esse judicent, sed quod juxta ordinatam rerum dependentiam in seipsis, unum ab intellectu nostro prius alio concipi debeat. Hic tamen observandum est inter ipsos Scholasticos, non admodum certam & constantem esse hanc doctrinam de hisce signis sive instantibus prioritatis & posterioritatis, quibus imbecilla nostra ratio sustentat se in consideratione decretorum Divinorum. Scotus, qui primarius est ad haec signa fabricanda artifex, videtur nonnullis non solum eadem posuisse priora & posteriora secundum nostrum intelligendi modum, sed insuper statuisse unum esse in ipso Deo prius natura alio; quasi hic ordo prioris & posterioris ex natura rei in ipsis Divinis actibus posset assignari. Sed cum attente lego quae Scotus de hisce signis tradit lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. unica, & lib. 3. dist. 7. qu. 4. & dist. 19. qu. unica, nihil aliud mihi docuisse videtur, quam esse in ipsis rebus aliquod fundamentum, unde nos concipiamus unum Dei decretum ordine quodam rationis nostrae alteri esse praeponendum. Jam vero ex adversa parte Occamus noster haec signa, quocunque modo considerata, negavit; In 1. dist. 9. qu. 3. & Bielus sententiam amplexus, haec signa oppugnavit, In 3. dist. 2. qu. 1. dub. 3. Prioritates in Divinis non sunt ponendae, sicut nec pluralitates actuum ordinatorum. Unus est enim actus in Divinis, re & ratione indistinctus, qui est ipsa essentia Divina; qua unica cognitione Deus praevidit Christi incarnationem, omnium electorum futuram beatitudinem, casum & reparationem; nec unum prius, aliud posterius: & mox addit, ne secundum nostram quidem considerationem talem ordinem prioritatis & posterioritatis concipi posse in decretis Divinis, ut talis consideratio non sit falsa speculatio. Dominicus Bannes, quamvis non omnino explodat haec signa cum Biele, perpendens tamen discordiam Theologorum in illis assignandis, Animadvertendum est, inquit, quam pro libito in negotiis praedestinationis & reprobationis multiplicentur instantia a Theologis, & quam parum illa conferant ad assignandam rationem differentiae inter praedestinatos & reprobos. Liceat itaque hic paucis monere, non esse nimis confidendum, aut tanquam certo dogmati adhaerescendum, ulli certo ordini decretorum Divinorum, sive a Protestantibus sive Pontificiis assignato, cum difficile sit duos reperire, sive inter nostros, sive inter adversarios, qui ad amussim per omnia consentiant in hac serie decretorum Divinorum describenda. Caveat itaque unusquisque ne talem considerationem praedestinationis & reprobationis inducat, quae vel Divinae justitiae, vel gratiae gratuitae adversatur: & cum non multum refert quo ordine prioritatis & posterioritatis haec decreta, quae reapse in Deo omnino simul sunt, secundum nostrum intelligendi modum distribuantur & disponantur.
pass_a: Second, although all acts in the Divine mind and will are eternal, and therefore are not separated even by the lightest moment of priority and posteriority; yet, from the side of the things themselves which God understands and has decreed, certain signs of priority and posteriority can be distinguished, according to our mode of understanding. And in this sense it is asked among theologians whether God first decreed to give the elect eternal life, or faith and obedience which lead to eternal life; and whether he first reprobated some and rejected them from eternal life before he foresaw them fallen and contaminated by sin. And hence it is that nearly all who have written on predestination and reprobation describe a certain series, and as it were a little table, in which they try to draw the order of the Divine decrees: not because they judge that according to the thing in God himself one is prior or posterior to another, but because according to the ordered dependence of things in themselves, one ought to be conceived by our intellect prior to another. Here yet it must be observed among the Scholastics themselves that this doctrine is not very certain and constant about these signs or instants of priority and posteriority by which our weak reason props itself in considering the Divine decrees. Scotus, who is the chief craftsman for fabricating these signs, seems to some not only to have placed the same as prior and posterior according to our mode of understanding, but further to have held that one is in God himself prior by nature to another; as if this order of prior and posterior could be assigned from the nature of the thing in the Divine acts themselves. But when I carefully read what Scotus hands down about these signs in book 1 distinction 41 unique question, and book 3 distinction 7 question 4 and distinction 19 unique question, he seems to me to have taught nothing else than that there is in the things themselves some foundation from which we conceive that one decree of God is to be set before another by a certain order of our reason. But now from the opposite side our Occam denied these signs, considered in whatever way; In 1 distinction 9 question 3, and Biel embracing the opinion attacked these signs, In 3 distinction 2 question 1 doubt 3: Priorities are not to be placed in Divine things, just as neither pluralities of ordered acts. For there is one act in Divine things, indistinct in reality and in reason, which is the Divine essence itself; by which one cognition God foresaw Christ's incarnation, the future beatitude of all the elect, the fall and the repair; nor one prior, another posterior: and soon he adds that not even according to our consideration can such an order of priority and posteriority be conceived in the Divine decrees, such that such consideration is not a false speculation. Dominic Bannes, although he does not altogether explode these signs with Biel, yet weighing the discord of theologians in assigning them, says, It must be noticed how at pleasure in the businesses of predestination and reprobation instants are multiplied by theologians, and how little those contribute to assigning the account of the difference between the predestined and the reprobate. Let it be allowed therefore here to warn in a few words that one must not trust too much, or cling as to a certain dogma, to any certain order of the Divine decrees, whether assigned by Protestants or by Pontificals, since it is hard to find two, whether among ours or among adversaries, who agree to the plumb-line through all things in describing this series of Divine decrees. Let each one therefore beware lest he bring in such a consideration of predestination and reprobation as stands against either Divine justice or free grace: and since it does not matter much in what order of priority and posteriority these decrees, which in reality in God are altogether at once, are distributed and arranged according to our mode of understanding.
pass_b: Second: although every act in God's mind and will is eternal, and so not parted even by the lightest instant of before and after, still, from the side of the things God understands and has decreed, certain signs of priority and posteriority can be marked — according to our way of understanding. In that sense theologians ask whether God first decreed to give the elect eternal life, or faith and obedience that lead to eternal life; and whether he first reprobated some and cast them from eternal life before he foresaw them fallen and stained by sin. Hence nearly everyone who has written on predestination and reprobation draws a kind of series, almost a little table, trying to sketch the order of the Divine decrees — not because they judge that in God himself one decree is really before or after another, but because, given the ordered dependence of the things in themselves, our intellect ought to conceive one before another. Yet among the Scholastics themselves this teaching about those signs or instants of before and after — props by which our weak reason steadies itself when it thinks of God's decrees — is not very fixed or constant. Scotus, the chief craftsman of these signs, seems to some not only to have set them as prior and posterior in our mode of understanding, but also to have held that one is prior by nature to another in God himself — as if that before-and-after order could be assigned from the nature of the thing in the Divine acts themselves. But when I read carefully what Scotus teaches on these signs (1 Sent. dist. 41 q. unica; 3 Sent. dist. 7 q. 4 and dist. 19 q. unica), he seems to me to teach only this: that in the things themselves there is some foundation from which we conceive that one decree of God is to be set before another by a certain order of our reason. From the other side our Occam denied these signs however considered (1 Sent. dist. 9 q. 3); and Biel, taking that view, attacked them (3 Sent. dist. 2 q. 1 dub. 3): "Priorities are not to be placed in Divine things, any more than pluralities of ordered acts. For there is one act in Divine things, indistinct in reality and in reason, which is the Divine essence itself; by that one cognition God foresaw Christ's incarnation, the future beatitude of all the elect, the fall and the repair — not one before, another after." And he adds at once that not even according to our consideration can such an order of before and after be conceived in the Divine decrees without that consideration becoming a false speculation. Dominic Báñez, though he does not wholly explode these signs with Biel, still weighs the theologians' discord in assigning them and says: notice how freely, in the business of predestination and reprobation, theologians multiply instants, and how little those help assign the account of the difference between the predestined and the reprobate. So let this brief warning stand: do not trust too much, or cling as to fixed dogma, to any certain order of the Divine decrees, whether drawn by Protestants or by Papal writers. It is hard to find two — among ours or among adversaries — who agree to the line in every point when they describe this series of Divine decrees. Let each take care not to bring in a view of predestination and reprobation that runs against Divine justice or free grace; and since these decrees are in reality altogether simultaneous in God, it matters little in what order of before and after we distribute and arrange them according to our mode of understanding.

lemmas.gloss: according to our mode of understanding

title: Prolegomena III: order founded in things' dependence; final vs efficient cause
latin: Tertio, quia propter imbecillitatem intellectus nostri cogimur saepenumero in materia praedestinationis explicanda, aliquid concipere ut prius, aliquid ut posterius (ut cum cogitamus Deum prius considerasse hominem ut lapsum, quam ut in Christo electum; vel cum affirmamus Deum prius hominem destinare ad vitam aeternam, quam ad gratiam efficacem) videamus qua in re fundetur hic ordo prioritatis & posterioritatis, quem consideramus in actibus Divinis. Non in ipsa scientia vel voluntate Dei secundum se: nam in Divinis, omnia sunt simul duratione. Fundatur itaque in ipsa rerum habitudine, prout una ex altera dependet. Quocirca secundum modum considerationis nostrae illud prius intelligitur in mente & voluntate Divina, a quo aliud pendet secundum ordinem causalitatis; illud posterius, quod pendet ab alio: si autem unum se habeat prorsus independenter ad aliud, neutrum dicendum est altero prius aut posterius. Dein, diligenter animadvertendum est, idem in diverso genere causae posse esse prius & posterius altero. Quod evidenter apparebit si causam effectivam seu dispositivam cum finali comparemus. Nam in genere causae finalis sanitas est prior pharmaco: movet etenim tum medicum ut det, tum aegrotum ut illud accipiat: At in genere causae effectivae pharmacum est prius sanitate: nam ejus virtute & efficacia aegrotus ad sanitatem reducitur. Sic in negotio praedestinationis, voluntas dandi vitam aeternam concipitur prior voluntate dandi efficacem gratiam in ordine causae finalis: nam ex intentione dandi vitam oritur decretum dandi talem gratiam: At in ordine causae effectivae prior est voluntas dandi gratiam, quae ideo datur ut ejus virtute & efficacia praeeunte homo perducatur ad gloriam. Atque hoc est quod a Philosopho innuitur, Ethic. 3. cap. 8. ubi docet, illud quod est ultimum in intentione, esse primum in executione; & e contra. Ratio hujus discriminis manifesta est; Quia in actu volendi & intendendi illud habet rationem causae, quod sui desiderio & amore movet efficientem ad talia media quaerenda & applicanda; in actu autem exsequendi illud habet rationem causae quod ipsum finem promovet, & operatur ad finis consecutionem. Sic Bannesius, Finis qui in intentione operantis habet rationem causae respectu mediorum, in exsecutione positus habet rationem effectus, & ipsa media habent rationem efficientis respectu ejus. Hoc valde observandum: nam cum secundum rem sit unicus & idem actus voluntatis in Deo, quo vult tam media quam finem, & finem per media, & media propter finem; tamen secundum nostrum intelligendi modum haec omnia distinguuntur: & hinc perplexae quaestiones, quid horum prius, quid posterius in voluntate Divina. Ut hisce occurratur, semper perpendendum est quem ordinem causalitatis res ipsae inter se habeant: nam eundem prioritatis habere intelliguntur. Hoc etiam addendum est, licet in actibus Divinae voluntatis quoad rem nulla sit prioritas vel posterioritas, tamen Deus non vult res creatas confuse & inordinate. Verum est quidem, in Deo non esse volitiones multas, nec unam alia priorem: sed unico tamen simplicissimo actu voluntatis suae voluit unam rem esse propter aliam, unam esse dependentem ab alia. Et hinc illa consideratio prioritatis & posterioritatis, quae proprie competit ipsis rebus, a nobis tribuitur ipsis decretis Divinis. Quapropter, quoties disceptatur sive de scientia Dei, quaerendo, ex duobus utrum hoc an illud prius sciverit; sive de voluntate, quaerendo ex duobus utrum hoc an illud prius decreverit; semper meminisse debetis, hanc prioritatem aut posterioritatem non inesse reapse, vere, & formaliter, ipsis actibus mentis & voluntatis Divinae, sed considerari ex parte rerum a Deo cognitarum & decretarum, inter quas Deus voluit esse veram & realem quandam prioritatem & posterioritatem. Atque haec pro instituto nostro, hac de re dixisse sufficiat.
pass_a: Third, because on account of the weakness of our intellect we are often forced, in explaining the matter of predestination, to conceive something as prior, something as posterior (as when we think that God first considered the human being as fallen, before as elected in Christ; or when we affirm that God first destines a human being to eternal life, before to efficacious grace) let us see in what thing this order of priority and posteriority is founded, which we consider in the Divine acts. Not in the knowledge or will of God according to itself: for in Divine things, all are simultaneous in duration. It is founded therefore in the very relation of things, insofar as one depends from another. Wherefore according to the mode of our consideration that is understood as prior in the Divine mind and will from which another hangs according to the order of causality; that as posterior which hangs from another: but if one stands altogether independently toward another, neither is to be said prior or posterior to the other. Next, it must carefully be noticed that the same thing in a diverse kind of cause can be prior and posterior to another. Which will appear evidently if we compare an effective or dispositive cause with a final one. For in the kind of final cause health is prior to the drug: for it moves both the physician to give it, and the sick person to receive it: But in the kind of effective cause the drug is prior to health: for by its virtue and efficacy the sick person is brought back to health. So in the business of predestination, the will of giving eternal life is conceived prior to the will of giving efficacious grace in the order of final cause: for from the intention of giving life arises the decree of giving such grace: But in the order of effective cause the will of giving grace is prior, which is therefore given so that by its virtue and efficacy going before the human being may be led through to glory. And this is what is hinted by the Philosopher, Ethics 3 chapter 8, where he teaches that that which is last in intention is first in execution; and the contrary. The reason of this difference is manifest; Because in the act of willing and intending that has the account of a cause which by desire and love of itself moves the efficient one to seek and apply such means; but in the act of executing that has the account of a cause which promotes the end itself, and works toward obtaining the end. So Bannes: The end which in the intention of the one working has the account of a cause with respect to the means, when placed in execution has the account of an effect, and the means themselves have the account of an efficient with respect to it. This must be greatly observed: for although according to the thing there is one and the same act of will in God, by which he wills both means and end, and the end through the means, and the means because of the end; yet according to our mode of understanding all these are distinguished: and hence the perplexed questions, which of these is prior, which posterior in the Divine will. That these may be met, it must always be weighed what order of causality the things themselves have among themselves: for they are understood to have the same of priority. This also must be added: although in the acts of the Divine will as to the thing there is no priority or posteriority, yet God does not will created things confusedly and without order. It is true indeed that in God there are not many volitions, nor one prior to another: but yet by one most simple act of his will he willed one thing to be because of another, one to be dependent from another. And hence that consideration of priority and posteriority, which properly belongs to the things themselves, is attributed by us to the Divine decrees themselves. Wherefore, whenever it is disputed either about God's knowledge, asking of two whether he knew this or that first; or about the will, asking of two whether he decreed this or that first; you must always remember that this priority or posteriority does not inhere in reality, truly, and formally in the acts themselves of the Divine mind and will, but is considered from the side of the things known and decreed by God, among which God willed there to be a certain true and real priority and posteriority. And these things, for our purpose, may suffice to have said on this matter.
pass_b: Third: because our intellect is weak, we are often forced, when explaining predestination, to conceive something as before and something as after — as when we think God first considered the human being as fallen, before as elect in Christ; or when we say God first destines a person to eternal life, before to efficacious grace. So let us see where this order of before and after, which we mark in the Divine acts, is founded. Not in God's knowledge or will considered in itself: in Divine things all are simultaneous in duration. It is founded in the relation of the things themselves, insofar as one depends on another. Therefore, in our mode of consideration, that is prior in the Divine mind and will from which another hangs in the order of causality; that is posterior which hangs from another. If one stands wholly independent of another, neither is prior or posterior to the other. Next, mark carefully: the same thing can be prior and posterior to another in different kinds of cause. Compare an efficient or dispositive cause with a final one. In the kind of final cause, health is prior to the drug: it moves the physician to give it and the sick person to take it. But in the kind of efficient cause the drug is prior to health: by its virtue and efficacy the sick person is brought back to health. So in predestination: the will to give eternal life is conceived prior to the will to give efficacious grace in the order of final cause — for from the intention of giving life arises the decree to give such grace. But in the order of efficient cause the will to give grace is prior, and grace is given so that by its virtue and efficacy going before, the person may be led through to glory. That is what the Philosopher hints (Ethics 3.8): what is last in intention is first in execution, and the reverse. The reason is plain. In the act of willing and intending, that has the account of a cause which by desire and love of itself moves the agent to seek and apply such means; but in the act of executing, that has the account of a cause which advances the end itself and works toward obtaining it. So Báñez: the end which in the agent's intention has the account of a cause with respect to the means, when set in execution has the account of an effect, and the means themselves have the account of an efficient cause toward it. Mark this well: although in reality there is one and the same act of will in God by which he wills both means and end, the end through the means, and the means for the end, still in our mode of understanding all these are distinguished — and hence the tangled questions which of them is prior or posterior in the Divine will. To meet those questions, always weigh what order of causality the things themselves have among themselves: they are understood to carry the same order of priority. Add this too: although in the acts of the Divine will as to the thing there is no before or after, God does not will created things in a confused, unordered heap. It is true that in God there are not many volitions, nor one prior to another; yet by one most simple act of his will he willed one thing to be for another, and one to depend on another. Hence that consideration of before and after which properly belongs to the things themselves is attributed by us to the Divine decrees. So whenever the dispute is about God's knowledge — asking of two which he knew first — or about his will — asking of two which he decreed first — always remember: this priority or posteriority does not inhere really, truly, and formally in the acts of the Divine mind and will themselves, but is considered from the side of the things God has known and decreed, among which he willed a true and real before and after. And for our purpose, that is enough on this point.
